blocks.content: A clean physics model can explain why a tighter turn asks more from a tire. It cannot tell you the grip, lean angle, or safe speed of a real gravel corner. Treat every numerical limit in this appendix as a model assumption, not a riding target.

### What changes in a turn

A bicycle needs tire grip to change direction. A tighter line or higher speed asks more of the tires. Braking and turning at the same time ask for grip in two directions. Loose stones, wet clay, cambers, bumps, tire construction, and pressure change the answer from one meter to the next.

That is why the same bend can feel easy on one ride and unsettled on another. Look for the exit, choose a line with room, and set a manageable speed before the turn. If the conditions change, slow the next attempt. There is no universal gravel lean angle or fixed percentage of a calculated maximum that makes the turn safe.

items.title: What a simple friction model leaves out
items.content:
In a classroom model, a tire has one friction coefficient and the road has one smooth radius. Real gravel has movable stones, ruts, changing load, tire deformation, and a rider who is steering, braking, and shifting position. Even a measured coefficient from another surface does not give you the grip beneath your front wheel now.

Use the model to understand a direction of change. A tighter turn usually demands more from the tires, and a less predictable surface calls for more room. Do not use it to calculate an entry speed or seek a lean-angle limit on the road.

blocks.content:
### Load moves when you brake

Braking shifts load toward the front wheel. That helps explain why both brakes matter and why a rear wheel can lock when it becomes light. The amount of grip available at either wheel still depends on the surface and the bike. Squeeze both brakes gradually on a straighter approach; do not assign a fixed front/rear split. Lesson 5 gives you a low-speed drill to feel this without chasing a short stop.

blocks.title: Turn the model into a field observation
blocks.description: Use observations from a familiar route instead of calculating a limit.

steps.detail: Record the surface, weather, tire setup, and whether you can see the exit.
Leave room to change course without entering traffic or a blind section.
At a comfortable pace, notice whether the bike tracks smoothly. Stop if it pushes, skids, or feels vague.
On a later ride, compare one change at a time. Do not turn a successful pass into a speed target.

blocks.title: Grip Notes, Not a Skid Test
blocks.description: On a flat, traffic-free loop, compare how a gentle bend feels on two clearly visible, stable surfaces. Keep speed low enough to stop easily and do not provoke a slide.

variants.label: A familiar easy loop
steps: Check the surface and a clear runout. Leave if there is traffic, hidden debris, or poor visibility.
Ride a wide bend at a comfortable pace. Notice the steering and how the tires track.
Repeat on another visible surface at the same easy pace. Do not tighten the turn or accelerate to find a limit.
Record the conditions and one handling difference. Stop if either tire feels unstable.

proof_gate.description: You can describe how two familiar surfaces felt without provoking a skid.
proof_gate.target: Record the conditions, line, and one handling observation for each surface

blocks.question: A formula estimates a maximum corner speed for “loose gravel.” What can you use that number for on a real ride?

options.text: Understanding that a tighter line can demand more grip, while choosing actual speed by visibility and conditions
Setting a guaranteed safe entry speed for every loose-gravel bend
Deciding when to force the front tire to slide during practice
Replacing the need to look through the exit

blocks.explanation: The model explains relationships, but its surface and tire assumptions do not hold across a real bend. Choose a conservative line and speed from what you can see and feel.

blocks.content: On your next easy ride, note one place where the surface or sightline changed your corner approach. Write down what you saw and what you did. Leave the calculator out of it.
